label: rem:knot-operator-basis-table
title: Knot operator action on NF basis pairs (symbolic in $q$)
html:
The NF decomposition of a knot operator determines which particle channel it opens on a given incoming pair — in particular whether its e^- coefficient is nonzero, i.e. whether it produces the electron channel. Tabulating these decompositions is therefore what realises the operator/channel selection that this appendix examines.

This appendix gives the complete NF decomposition of b_i \cdot \beta(T) \cdot b_j for every pair of NF basis elements and every tabulated operator T, symbolic in h = q - q^{-1}. All results are exact in q — numerical values appear only in the witness file for comparison at q_0.

Notation. h = q - q^{-1} (Hecke amplitude). The NF basis is \{\ \gamma,\ \sigma_0,\ \sigma_1,\ L_+,\ L_-,\ e^-\ \}, with e^- = \sigma_0\sigma_1\sigma_0. An operator is named by the closure of its braid word \beta(T): T_{2,n} is the word \sigma_0^n in the two-strand braid group B_2, whose closure is the (2,n) torus knot or link, and T_{2,n}^{(3)} is a word in the three-strand braid group B_3 whose closure is the same (2,n) torus link. Two such words are used: \sigma_0\sigma_1\sigma_0, whose closure is the Hopf link T(2,2), and (\sigma_0\sigma_1)^2\sigma_0, whose closure is the T(2,4) torus link. Both closures have two components, as every odd-length word in B_3 does.

Table L.1: NF basis multiplication table (T_{1,0} — identity operator)

The identity operator \beta(T_{1,0}) = \mathbf{1} gives the raw product b_i \cdot b_j. Every entry below is exact in h.

See Table 1.

Key observations:

  1. e^- channel universality under T_{2,2}^{(3)}: When the electron operator \beta(T_{2,2}^{(3)}) = e^- is inserted, the e^- coefficient is always nonzero (36/36 pairs). In contrast, under the identity operator T_{1,0}, only 19/36 pairs produce a nonzero e^- coefficient, leaving the channel closed for the remaining pairs.

  2. e^- \cdot e^- = \gamma + h\sigma_0 + h\sigma_1 + h^2 L_+ + h^2 L_- + (h^3+h)e^-: the self-product of the electron populates all six basis elements. The e^- coefficient is h^3 + h = h(h^2 + 1), which is always positive for q > 1.

  3. No negative coefficients appear in any basis product. Negative NF coefficients arise only from inverse elements (\sigma_i^{-1}), i.e., antiparticles.

Table L.2: T_{2,2}^{(3)} operator (electron)

\beta(T_{2,2}^{(3)}) = \sigma_0\sigma_1\sigma_0 = e^-, whose closure in B_3 is the Hopf link.

The product b_i \cdot e^- \cdot b_j is computed by composing the T_{1,0} table entries. Key entries (symbolic in h):

See Table 2.

All 36 pairs produce nonzero e^- coefficient under T_{2,2}^{(3)}.

The electron operator unconditionally opens the electron channel regardless of the incoming state, confirming T_{2,2}^{(3)} as the universal pair-production operator.

Table L.3: T_{2,1} operator (single crossing)

\beta(T_{2,1}) = \sigma_0.

See Table 3.

24/36 pairs produce e^- under T_{2,1} — but the photon-photon pair (\sigma_0 \cdot \sigma_0 \cdot \sigma_0) does not. T_{2,1} requires specific polarization content to open the electron channel.

Summary: operator channel opening

See Table 4.

T_{2,2}^{(3)} is the unique lowest-crossing operator that unconditionally produces the electron channel for all incoming pairs. Higher operators (T_{2,4}^{(3)}, etc.) also open all channels but at higher crossing energy cost (h^2 vs 1 for the photon-photon pair).
